title: The Compilation and Linking Pipeline
learning_outcomes: Explain the main idea behind the compilation and linking pipeline in your own words.
Apply the compilation and linking pipeline to a minimal C example and predict the result.
Identify a relevant boundary, portability assumption, or failure mode.

content.intro: This lesson explores The Compilation and Linking Pipeline through an original visual, a compact C example and a check you can perform locally.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding the compilation and linking pipeline helps you reason about C programs rather than relying on trial and error. It also helps you communicate assumptions, write safer code, and debug behavior across toolchains.

content_blocks.title: Compilation and linking pipeline
content_blocks.alt_text: Source → preprocessing → compilation → assembly → linking → executable.
content_blocks.caption: Original learning diagram; use it with the written explanation and compiler-specific checks.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
The Compilation and Linking Pipeline is studied as part of **Your First C Program and the Build Process**. Start with the contract: identify the inputs or program state, the rule C applies, and the observable result. Then check the behavior in a small, repeatable example.

The source curriculum also lists: Preprocessing, Compilation, Assembly, Linking. Keep these subtopics connected to the parent concept rather than treating them as unrelated trivia.

In C, details can depend on the selected language standard and implementation. Distinguish defined behavior from unspecified, implementation-defined, or undefined behavior, and consult the cited standard/compiler references when portability matters.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: For “The Compilation and Linking Pipeline”, write down the preconditions first. Identify valid inputs and boundaries, decide which C rule applies, then choose evidence that would falsify your assumption. Prefer a small test with a clear expected result and compile with diagnostics enabled.

content_blocks.title: Build pipeline starter
content_blocks.run_instructions: Compile with `cc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic main.c -o app`; the compiler driver invokes the necessary toolchain stages.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, rebuild with the same compiler flags, rerun the same inputs, and compare actual output with the stated result. For time-, platform-, or input-dependent examples, record the environment and do not expect identical values everywhere.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf lesson page does not run C code. Compile locally or use a separately deployed, isolated C runner; do not execute arbitrary learner code inside FastAPI.

content_blocks.title: Portability and safety check
content_blocks.text: Use a documented standard mode; treat compiler extensions as extensions, not ISO C guarantees. Check return values, buffer bounds, and object lifetime. This course example is draft material and needs code review on the target toolchain before publication.

task: In a scratch file, create one small example that demonstrates the compilation and linking pipeline. Explain the expected result before running it, compile with warnings enabled, and record one boundary case or portability question.
hints: Reduce the program to the smallest example that still shows the concept.
Write down the input, expected result, and assumptions before running it.
Check the official language/compiler reference and test a boundary case.
expected_output: A short, reproducible C example and explanation showing the compilation and linking pipeline, plus a note about one boundary or portability consideration.
common_mistakes: Treating the compilation and linking pipeline as a rule to memorize rather than a behavior to test.
Ignoring compiler warnings, input validity, or object lifetime.
Assuming behavior observed on one compiler is guaranteed by every C implementation.
summary: The Compilation and Linking Pipeline belongs to Your First C Program and the Build Process.
State the assumptions, verify the smallest example, and test boundaries.
Check the selected language standard and target compiler when portability matters.
